title: Electron sub-shells and orbitals
keyIdea: Each shell splits into sub-shells: s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6 and d holds 10. A sub-shell is made of orbitals, and one orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spins. An s orbital is a sphere; a p sub-shell has three dumbbell-shaped orbitals at right angles. Electrons fill the lowest energy first, in the order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d, and in a p sub-shell they go one per orbital before any pair. So carbon is 1s² 2s² 2p², and potassium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹.

kid: The shell model says shells hold 2, 8 and 8 electrons. Each shell is really split into sub-shells. They are called s, p and d. An s sub-shell holds 2 electrons. A p sub-shell holds 6. A d sub-shell holds 10. Shell 2 is 2s and 2p, so it holds 2 + 6 = 8.

A sub-shell is made of orbitals. An orbital is a region where an electron is likely to be found. One orbital holds 2 electrons at most, and they must spin in opposite directions. An s orbital is shaped like a sphere. A p sub-shell has three orbitals. Each one is a dumbbell, and they point along x, y and z.
Electrons fill the lowest energy first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, then 4s, then 3d. 4s comes before 3d because it is lower in energy. So potassium puts its 19th electron in 4s, not 3d.

In a p sub-shell, electrons go into separate orbitals first, with the same spin. They only pair up when each orbital has one. This is Hund's rule. Electrons repel, so they spread out. Carbon is written 1s² 2s² 2p². The small numbers count the electrons in each sub-shell, and they add up to the atomic number.
adult: This topic refines the 2, 8, 8 shell model that students meet at 14 to 16. Each shell n contains sub-shells (s, p, d), each sub-shell contains orbitals (1, 3 or 5), and each orbital holds up to two electrons of opposite spin. Configurations are written as 1s² 2s² 2p², with superscripts that sum to the atomic number.

The lab is an orbital box diagram ordered by energy. Learners build carbon, nitrogen and oxygen by tapping boxes, then add the 19th electron to argon to see 4s fill before 3d, and split chlorine's 2, 8, 7 into sub-shells. The lab never blocks a wrong fill. It flags an Aufbau slip or a Hund slip so the rule is found, not just told.

Common mistakes: thinking a p sub-shell holds 2 electrons like s, rather than 6 across three orbitals; pairing electrons in one p orbital before the others have one; putting the 19th electron in 3d because shell 3 is not yet full; and mixing up the shell number with the number of electrons. Another slip is to picture an orbital as a fixed path, like a planet's orbit, when it is a region of likely position.

To check understanding, ask for the configuration of an element from 1 to 20 and for the number of unpaired electrons in nitrogen or oxygen. Then ask why the sum of the superscripts must equal the atomic number.

familyTip: Use egg boxes as orbitals: each cup takes two eggs, one pointing up and one down. Ask your teenager to fill three cups for 2p with four eggs and explain why no cup gets a second egg until all three have one.

practice.prompt: What is the electron configuration of carbon (atomic number 6)?
practice.hint: Fill 1s, then 2s, then 2p, and make the small numbers add up to 6.
practice.explain: 1s takes 2, 2s takes 2, and the last 2 go into 2p: 1s² 2s² 2p². The superscripts add to 6, the atomic number.

practice.prompt: An element has 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s², then {n} electrons in 3p. What is its atomic number?
practice.hint: Add up all the electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2, then the 3p electrons.
practice.explain: Before 3p there are 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 12 electrons, so the atomic number is 12 + {n} = {=12+n}. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.

practice.prompt: How many unpaired electrons does nitrogen (1s² 2s² 2p³) have?
practice.hint: Three 2p orbitals, three electrons. Do they pair up or spread out?
practice.explain: By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons go one per orbital with parallel spins, so all three are unpaired.

practice.prompt: How many electrons can {k} full p sub-shells hold altogether?
practice.hint: A p sub-shell has three orbitals, and each orbital holds two electrons.
practice.explain: Each p sub-shell holds 3 × 2 = 6 electrons, so {k} of them hold 6 × {k} = {=6*k}.

practice.prompt: What shape is a p orbital?
choices: A dumbbell, two lobes on either side of the nucleus
practice.hint: Picture the shape that points along the x, y or z axis.
practice.explain: Each p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. The three p orbitals point along x, y and z. An s orbital is the sphere.

pool.prompt: Where does the 19th electron of potassium go?
choices: 4s, because 4s is lower in energy than 3d
pool.hint: Electrons fill the lowest energy sub-shell that still has room.
pool.explain: After 3p is full, 4s is lower in energy than 3d, so potassium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹.

pool.prompt: Which is the configuration of oxygen (atomic number 8)?
pool.hint: 2s holds only 2, and 2p can hold up to 6.
pool.explain: 1s² 2s² takes 4 electrons and the other 4 go into 2p: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. A p sub-shell holds 6, so nothing spills into 3s.

pool.prompt: How many unpaired electrons does oxygen (2p⁴) have?
pool.hint: Put one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals first, then pair the fourth.
pool.explain: Three electrons go one per 2p orbital, and the fourth pairs with one of them. That leaves 2 unpaired electrons.

pool.prompt: A neutral atom has 1s² 2s², then {n} electrons in 2p. How many electrons are in its second shell?
pool.hint: Shell 2 is made of the 2s and 2p sub-shells.
pool.explain: Shell 2 contains the 2 electrons in 2s and the {n} in 2p, so it holds 2 + {n} = {=2+n} electrons. 1s belongs to shell 1.

pool.prompt: What is the most electrons one orbital can hold?
pool.hint: Think of one box in the box diagram, not a whole sub-shell.
pool.explain: Any single orbital, s, p or d, holds at most 2 electrons, and they must have opposite spins. 6 is a whole p sub-shell; 8 is a whole shell 2.

pool.prompt: Chlorine is 2, 8, 7 in the shell model. How is its outer shell written with sub-shells?
pool.hint: 3s holds 2, and the rest go into 3p.
pool.explain: The 7 electrons in shell 3 are 3s² 3p⁵. An s sub-shell cannot hold more than 2, and 3p holds up to 6.

pool.prompt: Which statement about an s orbital is correct?
choices: It is a sphere centred on the nucleus
It is a fixed circular path the electron travels
pool.hint: An orbital is a region of likely position, not a track.
pool.explain: An s orbital is a spherical region where the electron is likely to be found. It is not a path like a planet's orbit.

pool.prompt: An atom has 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s², then {n} electrons in 3p. How many electrons are in its third shell?
pool.hint: Shell 3 here is the 3s and 3p sub-shells together.
pool.explain: Shell 3 holds the 2 electrons in 3s and the {n} in 3p: 2 + {n} = {=2+n}. In the shell model that is the outer-shell number.

visual.caption: Which configurations follow the filling order and the capacity of each sub-shell?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: see s and p orbital shapes, fill an orbital box diagram by tapping, find Hund's rule and why 4s fills before 3d.
